Package com.bilt.pos.session

Class CheckoutSession

java.lang.Object
com.bilt.pos.session.CheckoutSession
All Implemented Interfaces:
AutoCloseable
public final class CheckoutSession extends Object implements AutoCloseable
A loyalty-enabled terminal session on top of BiltNexoTerminalClient.

The session owns the basket, drives the terminal (or an external customer display), and orchestrates settlement — return allocations, rebate redemption, point redemption, stored value/card charge, and reward award — as a single flow. Every operation maps to standard Nexo Sale to POI 3.0 messages; the raw client remains available via getClient(), and the session-less device and admin operations (diagnostics, totals, printing, sound) via terminal().

Terminal operations are lazy: methods returning SessionResult (or SettlementFlow) send nothing until execute() (asynchronous, outcome through the registered handlers), executeSync(), get(), or getOrNull() (blocking) is invoked. Basket mutations are pure local compute — the automatic display refresh they trigger is asynchronous and conflated.

A session is bracketed on the terminal: the builder's start() announces it (Nexo Admin session start signal) and only hands out the session once the terminal acknowledged, and end() tells the terminal to discard the session-scoped data it accumulated. An ended session cannot be used or restarted. The register may run multiple sequential settlements and other operations before ending the bracket; SessionBasket.clear() starts a fresh basket after a successful settlement. Sessions are AutoCloseable, so try-with-resources sends the end signal even on exception paths.


 try (CheckoutSession session = CheckoutSession.builder()
         .client(client)
         .saleId("POS-LANE-3")
         .poiId("VictaLane-275839164")
         .currency("USD")
         .start()
         .get()) {
     ...
 }

Sessions are intended for use from a single register thread. abort() and updateInputDisplay(DisplayPayload) are the only methods that are safe to call from another thread.

    • basket

      public SessionBasket basket()
      The session's basket: item and tax mutations, batch edits, and snapshots. Mutations are rejected while a settlement or void is in flight, after the current basket has settled, or after the session has ended. Call SessionBasket.clear() after a successful settlement to begin another basket in the same session. Each mutation returns the updated snapshot without touching the wire; with autoDisplay enabled it also enqueues an asynchronous, conflated customer-display refresh (a failed refresh reports through onBackgroundError).

    • identifyMember

      public SessionResult<IdentifyResult> identifyMember(IdentifyOptions options)
      Prompts the customer on the terminal to identify themselves (Nexo CardAcquisition with loyalty handling).

      Lookup outcomes that simply leave the checkout without a member — not found, suspended, customer cancelled — are delivered to onSuccess with the corresponding IdentifyStatus; onError fires only for real failures.

      Identification remains available after a failed settlement, so a declined guest checkout can attach a member and retry with loyalty enabled.

    • settle

      public SettlementFlow settle()

    • settle

      public SettlementFlow settle(SettlementOptions options)
      Starts the settlement orchestration chain. Nothing is sent — and no precondition is verified — until the returned SettlementFlow's execute(), executeSync(), get(), or getOrNull() is invoked: the session must then be open with a non-empty, unconsumed basket. Sale lines are charged through the normal tender sequence; credit lines must be covered by the register-supplied refund allocations in SettlementOptions.

      Terminal-backed refund allocations carry the return-side itemization on the first PaymentRequest(Refund) leg only. Additional refund legs are amount-only because allocations are tender-level, not line-level.

      Refund allocations are not retried in the same settlement run. If one fails, already-committed refund allocation movements remain recorded, and the register retries by calling settle() again with the same committed allocation prefix. Charge-side failures after refund allocations use SettlementFlow.onError(java.util.function.Function<com.bilt.pos.session.SessionError, com.bilt.pos.session.settlement.SettlementOptions>) recovery options.

      A same-session void that already reversed one or more movements must be retried to completion before another settlement can replace its payment target.

    • refund

      public ReversalFlow<RefundResult> refund()
      Full linked refund of this session's completed payment. Also reverses the loyalty award when one ran — best-effort by default (override via ReversalFlow.onError(java.util.function.BiFunction<com.bilt.pos.session.ReversalStep, com.bilt.pos.session.SessionError, com.bilt.pos.session.ReversalDecision>)).

      Linked refunds reference a single transaction: after a split tender this is the card leg — use voidTransaction() to reverse both legs, or the stored value operations to return funds to the gift card. A refund reverses the card leg and award only; the sale's committed rebate and redemption movements are reversed by voidTransaction(). Once a refund has returned money the payment can no longer be voided; a tender skipped by an onError decision leaves it voidable, with an award the flow reversed remembered so nothing re-credits it. Once a void has partially reversed the payment's money legs, refunds are refused until the void is finished. To refund a sale taken by an earlier session, ring return lines into a new checkout session and provide refund allocations on SettlementOptions.

    • voidTransaction

      public ReversalFlow<VoidResult> voidTransaction()
      Reverses this session's completed payment: every movement it committed — the card and stored value legs (Nexo ReversalRequest), then the redemption, rebate, and award (their LoyaltyRequest refund types) — in that order. A checkout fully covered by rewards has no money leg; voiding it refunds the loyalty movements alone. To void a sale taken by an earlier session, use voidTransaction(OriginalSaleRecord).

      When a step fails, the flow's onError handler decides between retry, skip, and abort — see ReversalFlow for the default policy. A retried void resumes at the first movement still standing — reversed movements are never re-credited, and the retry's VoidResult describes only the movements that call sent. Until that retry succeeds, the session refuses basket().clear(), another settlement, and end() because each would discard the in-memory resume progress.

      On a session whose payment failed with an incomplete rollback, voidTransaction() finishes the unwind by retrying the reversals that did not go through. Not allowed once the payment has been refunded from this session — a void would return the full amount on top of the refund, so further returns must use refund(BigDecimal).

    • voidTransaction

      public ReversalFlow<VoidResult> voidTransaction(OriginalSaleRecord originalSale)
      Voids a prior sale by its persisted original-sale record. This is a whole-transaction void: every referenced card, stored value, rebate, redemption, and award movement is reversed in the same order as a same-session void. If the void partially fails, retry it on the same session instance because the in-memory reversed-step progress is what prevents already-reversed legs from being sent again; end() is refused until that retry succeeds. Mixed sale/return settlements should use settle(SettlementOptions) with refund allocations instead.

    • updateDisplay

      public SessionResult<Void> updateDisplay(Basket basket)
      Refreshes the customer display from the given basket snapshot using the configured DisplayRenderer. Failures are delivered through the returned result's onError, not the session's onBackgroundError — that handler is only for pushes the session initiates itself. Allowed until the session has ended.

    • abort

      public SessionResult<Void> abort()
      Aborts the in-flight operation. The session itself continues — an abort is a normal register maneuver (cancel the signature prompt, stop a tender to take a gift card first), not an abandonment; to abandon the checkout, end() the session.

      If a terminal operation is awaiting a response, a Nexo AbortRequest referencing it is sent (best-effort) to the device that is processing it. An aborted payment stops at its next step boundary, reverses the committed steps, and leaves the basket intact so settle() may retry (the thrown error carries SessionErrorCode.ABORTED). Aborted prompts (input, PIN, card reads, identification) deliver their aborted/cancelled outcome. With nothing in flight this is a no-op.

      Money-moving operations (refunds, stored value) always deliver their outcome even when the abort raced them: the movement may have completed on the terminal, and the register must know. Voids and the session lifecycle signals are never the abort's target — cancelling an in-flight end() would only strand the terminal's session-scoped data. An abort that lands after the payment completed leaves the transaction standing; use voidTransaction() to reverse it.

      Deliberately unordered: queued on the session's operation lane, the abort would wait on the very operation it cancels, so it overtakes it instead. Safe to call from any thread.

    • end

      public SessionResult<Void> end()
      Ends the session: tells the terminal to discard the session-scoped data it accumulated (Nexo Admin session end signal). After it succeeds, no session operation is allowed; create a new session to establish another terminal bracket.

      Refused while money is in flight, while a failed payment's rollback is incomplete, while a same-session or prior-sale void is partially complete, or while refund allocations from a failed settlement have committed — finish the unwind with voidTransaction() or retry settle() first, or the terminal/register state would be abandoned with money movements still unresolved. If the end signal fails, the session remains open so the call can be retried. A concurrent abort() never cancels an in-flight end — the exchange always settles.

    • close

      public void close()
      Best-effort end() for try-with-resources: a failure to send the end signal, or an unresolved movement that refuses end(), is logged, not thrown, and an already-ended session is left alone. Registers that need to react to a failed end should call end() directly.

      Blocking, and queued behind any in-flight operation — so with a callback executor configured, never call it from that executor's thread while operations may be in flight: the in-flight operation may need this thread for its handlers before it can finish, and both would wait forever. UI-driven teardown should use end().execute() with an onComplete instead; close() is for try-with-resources and process-exit paths.

      Specified by:
      close in interface AutoCloseable

    • updateInputDisplay

      public SessionResult<Void> updateInputDisplay(DisplayPayload payload)
      Replaces the display content of the input prompt currently awaiting a response (Nexo InputUpdate) — e.g. to update a countdown or amend the prompt while the customer decides.

      Because input calls block their calling thread, this must be invoked from a different thread; like abort() it is safe to do so. Fails with SessionErrorCode.INVALID_STATE when no input is in progress.

    • terminal

      public Terminal terminal()
      The device and admin operations of this session's terminal — diagnose(), getTotals(), reconcile(), print(), playSound()/stopSound() — built from this session's client, identifiers, and callback executor. Created lazily and cached; see Terminal.

      The terminal is deliberately independent of the session: it has its own operation thread and exchange, so its operations do not queue behind an in-flight payment (a connectivity check mid-payment works), they keep working after end(), and its close() does not touch the session. For the same reason abort() does not target terminal operations — they run on a separate exchange.
